extracted.intended_audience: university research administrators, technology transfer officers, contract administrators, and principal investigators involved with federally funded research
extracted.subtask_short: managing data/software rights under federal awards
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on federal rules (FAR, DFARS, agency supplements, OMB A-110) and TRIPs-related patent standards governing rights in technical data, computer software, copyrights, and related patentability/dispute provisions. Intended to help universities and practitioners identify, allocate, and protect rights when negotiating contracts/grants and when assessing international patent-related obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRIPs patentability requirements (Article 27(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents shall be available for 'any inventions, whether products or processes, in all fields of technology, provided that they are new, involve an inventive step, and are capable of industrial application.' A footnote states that terms inventive step and capable of industrial application may be deemed synonymous with nonobvious and useful, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Countries have interpreted the 'areas of technology' and 'industrial application' wording as allowing some subject-matter exclusions (e.g., business methods). Use this three-part test (novelty, inventive step/nonobviousness, industrial applicability/usefulness) when assessing TRIPs-compliant patentability; note national variation in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordre public and morality exclusions (TRIPs Articles 27(2),(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Member states may exclude inventions from patentability to protect ordre public or morality, including exceptions 'to protect human, animal, or plant life or to avoid serious prejudice to the environment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying morality exclusions, consider factors like public health benefit, containment and environmental release risk, and reduction of animal suffering. Example: EPO’s handling of the Harvard Oncomouse — narrowing claim scope (to mouse) and lab-restricted use supported patentability because the object was to save human life and reduce overall animal testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional provisions for developing countries (phasing in patent protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing countries were given transitional periods (five- or ten-year) to phase in provisions for patent protection for pharmaceutical and agricultural chemical products, with interim procedures allowing applications to be held in suspense while retaining filing dates and providing for limited marketing exclusivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Countries using transition options must provide exclusive marketing rights for applicants who filed domestically, secured an equivalent patent abroad, and obtained marketing approval elsewhere (see Articles 70(8),(9)). The Doha meeting extended implementation deadlines for least-developed countries (to Jan 1, 2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of country of origin / traditional knowledge (TRIPs review issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an ongoing debate whether patent applicants should be required to disclose the country of origin of genetic material or traditional knowledge incorporated in their applications so that source countries can ensure informed consent and fair compensation as called for under the Rio Convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions differ: some countries (Brazil, India, etc.) push for a disclosure requirement within the patent system; others (EU, US) prefer disclosure be addressed outside the patent system or by national legislation/contract. Expect unresolved international tension — factor in national rules and contractual obligations when drafting and filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory licensing and export mechanism (TRIPs Article 31 and Article 31bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 31 permits compulsory licensing under specified conditions. Article 31bis (amendment) provides that the requirement that a compulsory license be for predominantly domestic supply 'shall not apply' when the product is a pharmaceutical exported to address public health problems, subject to procedures and safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exporting under Article 31bis requires notifying the TRIPs Council, confirmation that the importing country cannot produce sufficient quantities, adequate remuneration to the patent owner, and safeguards to avoid abuse (e.g., special packaging/labeling where feasible). Follow the formal procedures and conditions set out in the annex and related WTO decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and national implementation (TRIPs Article 33)
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPs Article 33 requires patent term protection; implementation in the U.S. changed US patent term from seventeen years from grant to twenty years from filing (35 USC 154), with consequential procedural changes such as the introduction of provisional applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for differences in term calculation across jurisdictions (filing vs grant). In the U.S., provisional applications do not start the 20-year term but can be used to preserve priority for one year prior to filing a nonprovisional application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery/production of evidence in IP disputes (TRIPs Articles 34, 43, 47)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 43 requires judicial authorities, where reasonable evidence is presented and further evidence is under the control of the opposing party, to have the authority to order production of that evidence, subject to adequate protection of confidential information. Article 47 allows member countries to permit courts to order infringers to disclose identities of third parties involved in production or distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members may implement procedures to compel production and disclosure, but TRIPs does not mandate specific sanctions for noncompliance. Implement protective measures for confidential information when ordering disclosure or production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of protection for product-by-process and imported products (TRIPs Article 28 and national law differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPs' Article 28 sets a baseline for right to 'prevent third parties not having the owner's consent from the direct or indirect' use of the patented product; national implementations may be narrower or broader. For example, U.S. 35 USC 271(g) treats importation/sale of a product made abroad by a patented process as infringement unless materially changed; TRIPs language has been interpreted differently in various jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that TRIPs allows variation in national scope of protection; consult national statutes and case law (e.g., ITC decisions like Kinik Co v. ITC) to determine whether importation/sale of products made abroad using a patented process is actionable in a specific jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair and equitable patent prosecution procedures (TRIPs Article 62)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 62 extends principles of fair and equitable procedures to patent prosecution, specifically requiring 'no unnecessary complications or costs and no unreasonable time limits or delays' in patent prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent offices should streamline procedures; applicants and counsel should monitor prosecution timelines and procedural burdens to ensure compliance with TRIPs-derived expectations where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of counterfeit and pirated goods (TRIPs Article 61)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfeit trademark goods: 'any goods, including packaging, bearing without authorization a trademark which is identical to the trademark validly registered ... or which cannot be distinguished in its essential aspects from such trademark.' Pirated copyright goods: 'any goods which are copies made without the consent of the right holder ... and which are made directly or indirectly from an article where the making of the copy would have constituted an infringement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these definitions when assessing border measures, enforcement actions, and remedies under national law that implements TRIPs obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle: government unlimited rights to data under FAR (civilian contracts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under general FAR provisions, the government receives an unlimited license to data produced under research contracts enabling it to exercise the rights of the owner of the data, including reproducing, preparing derivative works, distributing copies to the public, and performing and displaying the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad government data license contrasts with the limited government-use license for inventions under Bayh-Dole. Check the contract type and clause language to determine whether the government truly acquires unlimited rights or whether statutory or agency-specific exceptions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAR 52.227-14 clause structure and need to verify clause text
rubrics_metrics.description: FAR 52.227-14 contains nine sections (Definitions; Allocation of Rights; Copyrights; Release, Publication, and Use of Data; Unauthorized Marking of Data; Omitted or Incorrect Markings; Protection of Limited Rights Data and Restricted Computer Software; Subcontracting; Relationship to Patents) and five alternate provisions. Contracts often cite clause numbers without text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities and contract administrators must have ready access to the full clause text (and any alternates) cited in agreements and carefully check the specific alternates included to align expectations and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities may establish copyright in scientific/technical articles without prior government approval
rubrics_metrics.description: FAR 52.227-14(c) permits contractors to establish, without prior government approval, copyright in scientific and technical articles that contain 'data first produced in the performance of the contract' if published in academic, technical, or professional journals, symposia proceedings, or similar media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions can pursue scholarly publication and claim copyright in such articles; verify that contract alternates or agency-specific rules do not impose additional requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAR permission for universities/colleges to claim copyright in data for basic/applied research contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: In contracts for basic or applied research performed solely by universities and colleges, FAR allows universities and colleges to claim copyright in any data (including computer software) produced under the contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This FAR provision protects academic dissemination and limits contractual restrictions on conduct/reporting of unclassified research, except as otherwise provided by U.S. statutes. Administrators should ensure contract language preserves publication rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of data categories under FAR 52.227-14(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: FAR defines 'data' as 'recorded information, regardless of form or the media.' Technical data are 'data which are of a scientific or technical nature.' It defines subsets including 'form, fit and function' data (enabling physical and functional interchangeability), 'limited rights data' (trade secrets or confidential commercial/financial information developed at private expense), 'computer software' (programs, databases, documentation), and 'restricted computer software' (software developed at private expense that is a trade secret or confidential).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correctly classifying deliverables as unlimited/limited/restricted or as form/fit/function is critical because classification determines the rights the government receives and protections the contractor retains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of FAR data rights: unlimited, limited, restricted
rubrics_metrics.description: FAR identifies 'unlimited rights' (government may use/disclose/reproduce/prepare derivative works/distribute/perform/display for any purpose and permit others to do so), 'limited rights' (as set forth in a limited rights notice in the clause), and 'restricted rights' (rights in restricted computer software set forth in a restricted rights notice or collateral agreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand each rights category and ensure proper marking and notice are used to preserve limited/restricted rights; failure to mark correctly can result in loss of protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of data that receive government unlimited rights under FAR 52.227-14(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government receives unlimited rights to: (1) data first produced in performance of the contract; (2) form, fit, and function data delivered under the contract; (3) manuals or instructional/training material for installation, operation, or routine maintenance; and (4) all other data delivered under the contract that are not marked with a limited or restricted legend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractors retain certain rights (use, publish, protect, correct, claim copyright) for some data first produced, depending on clause alternates. Unlimited rights are nonexclusive; when Alternate IV is included, contractors may assert ownership and license rights to third parties. Carefully assess which deliverables fall into the enumerated categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of rights depends on funding source and statement of work (DFARS and mixed funding)
rubrics_metrics.description: DFARS allocates rights and responsibilities for data produced under DOD contracts according to the source of funds used for development. If developed exclusively with government funds, the government is entitled to unlimited rights. Mixed government/private funding and the statement of work can change the rights allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the source(s) of funding for each element of development and craft the statement of work and contract terms to preserve intended rights. Note that DFARS does not make special provision for educational institutions; the DOD treats all contractors equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOE and NASA special rules for computer software where agency acquires contract rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Where DOE (and similarly NASA) acquires contract rights to data, it requires DOE permission to claim copyright for any computer software produced under the contract; NASA has a similar restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When negotiating DOE or NASA contracts, expect agency-specific limitations on asserting copyrights for software if the agency takes contract rights; plan negotiations and proposal-stage discussions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants: OMB A-110 and trend toward grantee copyright with federal reservation of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Under federal grants (per OMB Circular A-110 and agency practice), recipients generally may copyright data developed under the award, while the federal awarding agency reserves the right to reproduce, publish, or otherwise use the work for federal purposes. Federal Demonstration Partnership (FDP) agencies follow similar approaches with some agency-specific sharing/dissemination requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For grants, check agency-specific terms, FDP agency terms, and OMB A-110-derived conditions. Institutions should discuss rights at the proposal stage and understand any data-sharing or dissemination obligations attached to the award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracting officer obligations to include alternate provisions (FAR 27.409)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 27.409 provides instructions to contracting officers regarding the use of alternate sections contained in FAR 52.227-14 and summarizes situations in which the contracting officer is required to include alternates or other clauses (52.227-15 through 52.227-23) in a contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure contracting officers include the appropriate alternates for the specific procurement situation. University administrators should review solicitation clauses and negotiate alternates where necessary to protect institutional interests.
